newsitem.title: CHINA: Asian growth seen weaker as currency woes linger.
newsitem.headline: Asian growth seen weaker as currency woes linger.

text.p: Asian currency turmoil is not over and economists are making downward revisions to economic growth projections for the worst-hit nations as they reassess the damage.

"The matter is still not settled," George Leung, economic adviser at Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp, said on Monday. "I think the trend is for Asian currencies to depreciate until the economies start to recover."

The depreciations will occur as Asian nations, grapple with the consequences of more flexible exchange rate regimes, which have caused a rethink in Asian markets and economies following intense currency speculation.

"We've seen a a run on the (Singapore) dollar, which used to be a safe haven," one analyst said. "That is a sea change. What we're seeing here is money leaving Asia rather than moving around some of these smaller countries."
Asian currencies continued to feel the heat on Monday from currency contagion ignited by the July 2 flotation of the Thai baht. The Philippines peso was floated on July 11.
The baht came under pressure on worries stemming from gloom over the outlook for Thailand's economic development.
The Singapore dollar was stable on Monday but the Indonesian rupiah came under attack, the Malaysian ringgit was unstable and the Philippines central bank intervened to support the peso.
The Thai baht has depreciated more than 18 percent since January, the Indonesian rupiah has shed more than 12 percent of its value over the same period and the Philippine peso has fallen 8.6 percent.
In the meantime, higher interest rates used to counter currency speculators will depress overall economic growth, as will rising debt service costs.
"We have certainly changed our numbers for the Philippines and Thailand quite drastically," said Kevin Chan, assistant director at ING Barings in Hong Kong.
Revised economic projections are still being calculated, but most economists said the benefits of a weaker currency -- such as stronger exports -- will take "some quarters" to materialise.

"It's really a little bit early to say how long before things improve. It depends crucially how long this (speculation) goes on and how quickly rates can go back to normal," said another economist, who declined to be named.
In the meantime, inflation will rise, and trade and current account deficits will widen from already high levels.

"We are having to revise our expectations for imports, exports, interest rates, inflation," ING Baring's Chan said. "All the economic variables are interrelated. You can't change one without the others."

ING Barings now sees slower Thai growth from earlier projections of 5.2 percent, which was already weaker compared with teh 1996 growth rate of 6.7 percent. Inflation will also rise above forecasts of 4.7 percent, Chan said.

The current account deficit as a percentage of gross domestic product will widen beyond earlier expectations of 6.7 percent this year, Chan said. Thailand's current account deficit was the widest in the world in 1996 at 8.7 percent.

In the Philippines, economic growth will fall from earlier forecasts of 5.9 percent, Chan said. Inflation will reach above expectations of 8.4 percent while the current account deficit as a percentage of GDP will fail to narrow to earlier expectations of 4.6 percent.
HSBC's Leung was making similar revisions, although his were less severe. Growth, inflation and current account deficits would alter "by just a few percentage points," he said.
However, Leung warned that the currency uncertainty would damage sentiment and this could repel foreign investment, which would have longer-term implications.
